1aynaad:366: The core problem with AI Coding Agent memory systems is not "what to remember", but "at what cost and at which layer it gets recalled". This framing turns memory from a storage-capacity problem into a recall-path design problem. Each of the four layers has different latency and cost characteristics: hot memory (MEMORY.md/USER.md) is injected into the system prompt as a frozen snapshot at the start of every session — zero latency but a persistent drain on the prompt token budget; session_search queries the database via FTS5 full-text search, with controllable cost but dependence on summary quality; skills are an on-demand index that only expands when actually executed; external user models use asynchronous prefetch and do not block the current turn. This layering aligns exactly with the Agent Harness working-set idea: the window only holds the working set actually needed for the current turn, and assets outside the window are reached through explicit recall paths. Memory layering is a natural extension of context governance, not an independent pile of capabilities.

1mj9t72:315: Skills are called procedural memory, and this naming reveals their true design intent: they are not logs of "what happened this time", but SOPs encoding "how to do this type of task next time". Factual memory answers "what is the environment", session retrieval answers "what happened before", and Skills answer "when hitting a problem of type X, what steps should be followed". If a team repeatedly runs into the same type of problem, encoding the solution as a skill rather than leaving it in chat history is true knowledge accumulation. Skills also introduce a unique risk: once mistaken experience is solidified, it is harder to correct than an ordinary mistake, because the skill will keep triggering in the future. Therefore skills must have explicit lifecycle management: create, update, delete, annotate applicable scope, and ideally include verification steps and failure modes.

1tqia55:292: Long-session compression is a challenge every long-running Agent faces. Compression itself is not surprising; the hard part is whether the Agent can still work afterward. If key state is not actively migrated to durable memory before compression, it is permanently lost after compression. The memory flush mechanism embeds state-migration logic before compression: before history is thinned out, the Agent is given a dedicated chance to write facts worth long-term retention (user preferences, repeated corrections, stable conventions) into the hot memory layer, and only then is compression allowed to execute. This is essentially a checkpoint before the history is thinned. This principle applies to any Agent system with compression: there must be an explicit state-migration opportunity before compression, otherwise "remembering" is empty talk in engineering.

zim2b1:335: Hot memory is a short card injected into the system prompt at the start of every session. Designing the boundary of this layer is more critical than jumping straight to a vector store. Hot memory must be small enough (MEMORY.md defaults to 2,200 characters; USER.md to 1,375 characters) and hold only high-value facts needed every turn: user preferences, stable environment conventions, recurring pitfalls and corrections. The character limit rather than a token limit is a simple but correct engineering choice: it makes hot-memory size control completely independent of any specific model's tokenizer, so hot-memory capacity remains valid when migrating across models. The write boundary is equally important. Hot memory encourages storing user preferences, environment facts, and stable conventions; it explicitly discourages storing current task progress, this session's results, temporary TODOs, and one-off debugging paths. Once memory content enters the system prompt, it becomes part of the prompt supply chain and must be handled with the same level of input validation and permission management.
